\section[o obstáculo]{o obstáculo — the obstacle}

\label{lesson:PT-C353-obstaculo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the excuse, then the Portuguese for to justify.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o obstáculo}
\textbf{o obstáculo} — \textquotedblleft{}the obstacle\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O maior obstáculo é a língua.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The biggest obstacle is the language.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Superar um obstáculo} — to overcome an obstacle.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{obstáculo} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{obstāculum} \textquotedblleft{}a hindrance, an obstacle\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB, Lewis \& Short), from \emph{obstāre} \textquotedblleft{}to stand in the way\textquotedblright{}, built on \emph{stāre} \textquotedblleft{}to stand\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o obstáculo}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o obstáculo}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{o obstáculo}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for the excuse, then the Portuguese for to justify, then say \emph{o obstáculo} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does o obstáculo mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The obstacle\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[o desafio]{o desafio — the challenge; the match (in sport)}

\label{lesson:PT-C353-desafio}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to justify, then the Portuguese for the obstacle.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o desafio}
\textbf{o desafio} — \textquotedblleft{}the challenge; the match (in sport)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Aprender uma língua nova é um desafio.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Learning a new language is a challenge.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Aceitar um desafio} — to take up a challenge. In Portugal also a football match.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{desafio} is built on \emph{desafiar} \textquotedblleft{}to challenge\textquotedblright{}, usually traced to \emph{des-} and \emph{fiar} \textquotedblleft{}to trust\textquotedblright{}, which EtymDB derives from Vulgar Latin \emph{fīdāre}, a form of Latin \emph{fīdere} \textquotedblleft{}to trust\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB, Lewis \& Short): to challenge is to break the bond of trust.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to justify, then the Portuguese for the obstacle, then say \emph{o desafio} again

\section[impedir]{impedir — to prevent, to stop (from)}

\label{lesson:PT-C353-impedir}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the obstacle, then the Portuguese for the challenge.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: impedir}
\textbf{impedir} — \textquotedblleft{}to prevent, to stop (from)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A chuva impediu-nos de sair.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The rain stopped us from going out.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Impedir alguém de fazer algo} — to prevent someone from doing something.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{impedir} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{impedīre} \textquotedblleft{}to entangle, to hinder\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built from \emph{in} and \emph{pēs, pedis} \textquotedblleft{}foot\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short): to catch someone by the feet.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[dificultar]{dificultar — to make difficult, to hinder}

\label{lesson:PT-C353-dificultar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the challenge, then the Portuguese for to prevent.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: dificultar}
\textbf{dificultar} — \textquotedblleft{}to make difficult, to hinder\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O trânsito dificultou a viagem.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The traffic made the journey difficult.}
\end{quote}

Built on \emph{difícil}: to make hard.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{dificultar} comes from Latin \emph{difficultāre} (EtymDB), built on \emph{difficultās} \textquotedblleft{}difficulty, trouble\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), from \emph{difficilis} \textquotedblleft{}hard\textquotedblright{}, on \emph{facilis} \textquotedblleft{}easy\textquotedblright{} with \emph{dis-}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[favorecer]{favorecer — to favour, to help along}

\label{lesson:PT-C353-favorecer}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to prevent, then the Portuguese for to make difficult.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: favorecer}
\textbf{favorecer} — \textquotedblleft{}to favour, to help along\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O bom tempo favoreceu o turismo este verão.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The good weather helped tourism this summer.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Ser favorecido} — to be favoured.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{favorecer} is built on \emph{favor} \textquotedblleft{}favour\textquotedblright{}, from Latin \emph{favor} \textquotedblleft{}favour, goodwill, inclination\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), with the verb ending \emph{-ecer}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
